{{Short description|Cryptogram of 18th-century pirate Olivier Levasseur}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=August 2025}}

[[Image:Crypto de la buse.jpg|right|thumb|The cryptogram of Olivier Levasseur]]

The '''cryptogram of Olivier Levasseur''' (also known as '''''La Buse'' cryptogram''') is a 17-line [[pigpen cipher]] allegedly created by 18th-century French [[Piracy|pirate]] [[Olivier Levasseur]], and first attested by French historian and librarian {{ill|Charles de La Roncière|fr|Charles de La Roncière}} in his 1934 paperback novel ''[[Le Flibustier Mystérieux: Histoire d'un trésor caché]]''.<ref name="Dahlke-2024">{{Cite conference |last=Dahlke |first=Carola |year=2024 |title=Demystifying La Buse's Cryptogram and the Fiery Cross of Goa |url=https://dspace.ut.ee/server/api/core/bitstreams/d9f57dc9-f585-4550-b2a3-6ac8534b1557/content |publisher=Tartu University Library |pages=1–9 |doi=10.58009/aere-perennius0089 |access-date=5 June 2025 |doi-access=free |hdl-access=free |book-title=Proceedings of the 7th International Conference on Historical Cryptology (HistoCrypt 2024) |hdl=10062/98464}}</ref><ref name="Roncière-1934">{{Cite book |last=Roncière |first=Ch. De La |url=https://online.flipbuilder.com/kapali_patrimoine/ygev/index.html |title=Le Flibuster Mystérieux: Histoire d'un trésor cache |date=1934 |publisher=Edité par "Le Masque", Paris |language=Old French |edition=Sixth |pages=2–12 |ref=laronciere |access-date=5 June 2025}}</ref>

La Roncière claimed the [[cryptogram]] and the treasure to which it purportedly refers originated from a [[John Taylor (pirate)#History|raid]] on the Portuguese cargo ship ''Nossa Senhora do Cabo'' in 1721 by a group of pirates including Levasseur, [[Jasper Seagar]] and [[John Taylor (pirate)|Captain John Taylor]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dimri |first=Bipin |date=12 May 2022 |title=Can You Find the Treasure? The Unsolved Code of the Pirate Levasseur |url=https://www.historicmysteries.com/unexplained-mysteries/levasseur-treasure/24304/ |publisher=Stella Novus LTD |access-date=5 June 2025 |ref=HMLEVA |website=Historic Mysteries}}</ref> On board the ''Nossa Senhora'' was a large amount of valuable cargo, along with the [[Luís de Meneses, 1st Marquis of Louriçal|Viceroy of Goa]], who was later released for ransom. With a share of the loot and currency, Levasseur went into hiding for nine years until he was captured in July 1730, when he was executed.<ref name="Dahlke-2024" /> A popular legend claims that immediately before his execution, Levasseur threw a piece of paper into the watching crowd and shouted {{langx|fr|"Mes trésors à qui saura comprendre"|lit=My treasures to those who will know how to understand}}.<ref name="Decayeux">{{Cite web |last=Decayeux |first=Alain |title=OLIVIER LEVASSEUR aka LA BUSE |url=https://www.pirates-privateers.com/olivier-levasseur-la-buse.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250209011234/https://www.pirates-privateers.com/olivier-levasseur-la-buse.htm |archive-date=9 February 2025 |access-date=5 June 2025 |website=Pirates-Privateers |ref=P-PLABUSE}}</ref> The written cryptogram supposedly ended up in the possession of La Roncière, who then decrypted it in his 1934 novel.<ref name="Dahlke-2024" /> Though the 1721 raid of ''Nossa Senhora'' by Levasseur and his associates is well attested by historians, no concrete evidence for the treasure's existence has ever been uncovered, despite many searches and investigations, which suggests the cryptogram may have been an invention of La Roncière for his novel.<ref name="Dahlke-2024" />

==Historical background==
===Raid of the ''Nossa Senhora''===
[[Olivier Levasseur]] was born in [[Calais]] in 1688. Levasseur received a high standard of education in his early life and later became known for being a ruthless and efficient pirate.<ref name="Dahlke-2024" />{{rp|1}}<ref name="Golden Age of Piracy" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Nelson |first=Laura |date=2015 |title=Sam Bellamy & Olivier Levasseur Two Pirates Just Kickin' Around the Caribbean |url=http://www.cindyvallar.com/BellamyLevasseur.html |access-date=6 June 2025 |website=Pirates and Privateers. The History of Maritime Piracy |ref=PAPLN}}</ref> Receiving a [[letter of marque]] from [[Louis XIV]],<ref name="Golden Age of Piracy"/> he became a [[privateer]] during the [[War of the Spanish Succession]] as a raider of enemy ships in the Caribbean for the French. Early on, Levasseur decided to serve himself rather than his government and began accumulating wealth as a pirate, earning himself the nickname of "La Buse".<ref name="De Abreu-2023">{{Cite web |last=De Abreu |first=Kristine |date=25 January 2023 |title=Exploration Mysteries: The Treasure of Olivier Levasseur |url=https://explorersweb.com/exploration-mysteries-treasure-olivier-levasseur/ |access-date=5 June 2025 |website=Explorersweb |ref=EXWLAB}}</ref> In 1716, during what is now known as the [[Golden Age of Piracy]], Levasseur, using the alias of Louis de Boure and working with [[Benjamin Hornigold]] and [[Samuel Bellamy|Samuel "Black Sam" Bellamy]], began to build a reputation as an efficient pirate.<ref name="Golden Age of Piracy">{{Cite web |title=Olivier Levasseur |url=https://goldenageofpiracy.org/pirates/pirate-rounders/olivier-levasseur.php |access-date=5 June 2025 |website=Golden Age of Piracy |publisher=Sabalico |ref=GAOPOL}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Hostin |first=Geraldo |date=2020 |title=The Identification of the Pirate and Shipwreck |url=https://www.mahsnet.org/news/newsletters/V32-2_Fall_21.pdf |access-date=5 June 2025 |magazine=MAHS News |publisher=Maritime Archaeological and Historical Society |pages=7–12 |volume=32 |issue=2 |doi=10.13140/RG.2.2.18398.59201/1 |doi-broken-date=1 November 2025 }}</ref>

On 8 April 1721, Levasseur, Jasper Seagar and Captain John Taylor, aboard the [[sailing ships]] ''Victory'' and ''Cassandra'', arrived at the [[Réunion|island of Reunion]]. There they found the Portuguese [[cargo ship]] ''Nossa Senhora do Cabo'' anchored at [[Saint-Denis, Réunion|Saint-Denis]]. The masts and two-thirds of the cannons were reportedly missing upon discovery, with the ship damaged in a recent passing storm.<ref name="Dahlke-2024" />{{rp|5}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lazinby |first=Richard |year=1722 |title=Richard Lazinby's Account of the Proceedings of the Pirates Who Boarded the Cassandra in 1719 |journal=Letters 97–99, IOR/E/1/13 Ff. 165–178v |location=London |publisher=British Library}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Clifford |first1=Brandon A. |last2=Agostini |first2=Mark R. |title=From Goa to Sainte-Marie: An Archaeological Case for the Identification of the Nossa Senhora do Cabo |url=https://shipwreckcenter.org/sainte-marie-madagascar/ |website=Shipwreck Center |access-date=26 October 2025 |ref=SCBACMRA}}</ref>

The band of pirates boarded the ''Nossa Senhora'' without resistance and allegedly discovered a trove of valuables including gold and silver bars, precious silks and gemstones, spices and furniture collectively valued in the millions of the [[French livre|local currency]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Travers |first=Tim |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gu8SDQAAQBAJ&q=taylor |title=Pirates: A History: A History |date=2012 |publisher=The History Press |isbn=9780752488271 |location=Charleston SC |pages=130–132 |language=en |accessdate=5 June 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Watkins |first=Richard |date=22 March 2023 |title=Treasure hunt: Discover a buried secret on your next Seychelles yacht charter |url=https://www.yachtcharterfleet.com/destination/article/treasure-hunt-discover-a-buried-secret-on-your-next-seychelles-yacht-charter-16009.htm |access-date=5 June 2025 |website=YachtCharterFleet |ref=YCFTH}}</ref> Along with the highly valuable treasure, the ''Nossa Senhora'' was ferrying [[Luís de Meneses, 1st Marquis of Louriçal]] and Viceroy of Goa, en route to [[Portugal]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wilson |first=David |date=December 2018 |title=From the Caribbean to Craignish: Imperial Authority and Piratical Voyages in the Early-Eighteenth-Century Atlantic Commons |url=https://strathprints.strath.ac.uk/70013/1/Wilson_Itinerario_2018_imperial_authority_and_piratical_voyages_in_the_early_eighteenth_century.pdf |journal=[[Itinerario]] |volume=42 |issue=3 |pages=430–460 |doi=10.1017/S016511531800061X |access-date=5 June 2025 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Before splitting the treasure and going into hiding, the pirates released the viceroy in exchange for a ransom.<ref name="Dahlke-2024" />{{rp|5}}
[[Image:Retrato de D. Luís Carlos Inácio Xavier de Menezes (séc. XVIII) - Pompeo Batoni.png|right|thumb|The Viceroy of Goa, [[Luís de Meneses, 1st Marquis of Louriçal]], who was on board the ''Nossa Senhora'' at the time of the raid]]

===The Fiery Cross of Goa===
An artifact said to be on board the ''Nossa Senhora'' was the golden Fiery Cross of Goa, from the [[Se Cathedral]].<ref name="Dahlke-2024" />{{rp|1}}<ref name="Herald Goa-2023">{{cite web |title=One Piece, Olivier Levasseur and the Fiery Cross of Goa |url=https://www.heraldgoa.in/cafe/one-piece-olivier-levasseur-and-the-fiery-cross-of-goa/44783/ |publisher=[[Herald Goa]] |date=7 July 2023 |access-date=29 November 2025 |ref=HG}}</ref> [[Goa]] is a state on the southwestern coast of [[India]]'s [[Konkan region]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=13 October 2023 |title=Goa Beyond Beaches : Spices Gardens and Konkan Cuisine |url=https://enrouteindianhistory.com/goa-beyond-beaches-spice-gardens-and-konkan-cuisine/ |access-date=18 June 2025 |website=Enroute Indian History |ref=EIHGOA}}</ref> It was a colony of [[Portugal]] from the 16th century until 1961, when it was [[Annexation of Goa|annexed]] by India.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Faleiro |first=Valmiki |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GYLyEAAAQBAJ |title=Goa, 1961: The Complete Story of Nationalism and Integration |date=24 July 2023 |publisher=Penguin Random House India Private Limited |isbn=978-93-5708-175-7 |language=en}}</ref> The Cross itself was described as being as much as seven feet tall and covered with high-value [[gemstones]] such as [[emerald]]s, [[ruby|rubies]] and [[diamond]]s. Being made of gold, the Cross would have required multiple individuals to carry it.<ref name="Herald Goa-2023"/> Despite the legend of the Cross existing now, it is not mentioned by name anywhere prior to La Roncière's 1934 novel, which itself does not mention the Cross.<ref name="Dahlke-2024" />{{rp|6}}

===Execution of Levasseur===
Nine years after the ''Nossa Senhora'' raid, in 1730, Levasseur was captured and transported to [[Réunion|Reunion island]] by Captain d'Hermitte of the naval vessel ''La Meduse'',{{efn|Not to be confused with the [[French frigate Méduse (1810)|French frigate of the same name]] that sank in 1816.}} followed by [[execution]] for his crimes.<ref name="Fleming-1958">{{Cite news |last=Fleming |first=Ian |date=17 August 1958 |title=Treasure Hunt in Eden |url=https://quarterdeck.commanderbond.net/t/ian-flemings-adventure-journalism/1417/25 |access-date=24 June 2025 |work=[[The Sunday Times]] |quote=Includes contribution by R. H. Wilkins}}</ref> However, the details surrounding what took place leading up to his execution vary by source. The most famous story of Levasseur's execution speaks of him throwing a piece of paper with a [[Pigpen cipher|17-line pigpen cipher]] written on it to the watching crowd. This message is said to encrypt the location of his share of the treasure, stolen during the raid on the ''Nossa Senhora''. As he threw it, Levasseur reportedly shouted {{langx|fr|"Mes trésors à qui saura comprendre"|lit=My treasures to he who will know how to understand}}.<ref name="Decayeux" /> Some accounts say that the cryptogram paper was concealed within a necklace, though neither the necklace nor the original paper containing the cryptogram have ever been seen.<ref name="Dahlke-2024" /><ref name="De Abreu-2023" />

==Cryptogram==
===''The Clavicles of Solomon''===
In 1934, {{ill|Charles de La Roncière|fr|Charles de La Roncière}} wrote a novel, ''Le Flibustier Mystérieux: Histoire d'un trésor caché'' ({{langx|en|The Mysterious Buccaneer: The Story of a Hidden Treasure}}), for the Parisian publishing house Le Masque.<ref name="Dahlke-2024" /> Written entirely in French, ''Le Flibustier Mystérieux'' begins by presenting the idea of ''[[Key of Solomon|The Clavicles of Solomon]]'' as a non-fiction [[Kabbalah|cabalistic manual]], both authored by and passed down from [[King Solomon]] himself to his son [[Rehoboam]] ("Roboam" in the novel). A testament left to Rehoboam by King Solomon engraved on the bark of a tree read, {{langx|fr|"J'obtins par surcroît la jouissance de tous les trésors célestes et la connaissance de toutes choses naturelles. C'est, mon fils, par ce moyen que je possède toutes les vertus et richesses dont tu me vois jouir à présent."|lit=I also obtained the enjoyment of all heavenly treasures and knowledge of all natural things. It is, my son, by this means that I possess all the virtues and riches which you see me enjoying presently.}} La Roncière then draws on poet [[Edgar Allan Poe]]'s ''[[The Gold-Bug]]'', writing that when heated the poetic instruction written in an opaque ink would appear on the [[parchment]], revealing the existence of a hiding place.<ref name="Roncière-1934" />{{Rp|3}}
[[File:La Roncière translation.png|right|thumb|Translation by Charles de La Roncière of [[Olivier Levasseur]]'s cryptogram signs.]]
La Roncière then pivots back to ''The Clavicles of Solomon'', introducing a young woman and an island in the Indian Ocean, unnamed so that the treasure remains undiscovered. Three bodies are observed, two in [[coffins]] with a [[Earring#Hoop earrings|ring]] on the left ear, identifiable as sailors.<ref name="Roncière-1934" />{{rp|5}}<ref name="The Townsville Daily Bulletin-1950">{{Cite news |date=16 January 1950 |title=Treasure Hunt in Indian Ocean |url=https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/63474922 |access-date=24 June 2025 |work=The Townsville Daily Bulletin}}</ref> The young woman is then handed two documents from the landowner, one being a cryptogram, which could only be deciphered by using the characters of ''The Clavicles of Solomon''.<ref name="Roncière-1934" />{{Rp|5}}<ref name="Bath-2013">{{cite book |last1=Bath |first1=G.J. |title=Maps, Mystery and Interpretation Vol 2. Oak Island Speculation |url=https://www.gjbath.com/Misc/LaBuse.htm |publisher=KeyPress |year=2013 |access-date=2 November 2025 |ref=GJBBT}}</ref> The young woman wrote to [[La Bibliothèque Nationale de France]], asking for access to ''The Clavicles of Solomon''. A connection between the cabalistic signs and the signs on Levasseur's cryptogram was assumed, however it is left ambiguous as to whether this was surmised by La Roncière or the young woman.<ref>{{cite book |title=Explorateurs et pionniers français |url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k7055109d/f28.item |year=1941 |page=26 |last1=Roncière |first1= Ch. De La |publisher=L'Alliance du livre (Paris) |access-date=7 December 2025 |volume=1}}</ref> La Roncière presents this in ''Le Flibustier Mystérieux'', with further context provided in his 1941 book ''Explorateurs et pionniers français''.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pelling |first1=Nick |title=Charles de la Ronciere's thoughts on Le Flibustier Mysterieux… |url=https://ciphermysteries.com/2023/12/10/charles-de-la-roncieres-thoughts-on-le-flibustier-mysterieux |website=Cipher Mysteries |access-date=7 December 2025 |date=10 December 2023 |ref=CMNP101223}}</ref>

===The Cryptogram of Olivier Levasseur===
The next section of the novel (pages six through twelve), titled {{langx|fr|"Le Cryptogramme Du Forban"|lit=The Cryptogram of the Privateer}}, discusses the cryptogram which has come to be attributed to Levasseur's share of the treasure from the 1721 raid on the ''Nossa Senhora''. The sixth page of ''Le Flibustier Mystérieux'' provides a description of the written cryptogram symbolage and their attributed values, translated by La Roncière, on the seventh page. La Roncière writes that Levasseur's cryptogram uses handwritten signs, reminiscent of [[Hebrew letters]], each of which represent two letters, known as a [[Digraph (orthography)|digraph]]. The first of these letters is usually removed, leaving only the second letter readable.<ref name="Roncière-1934" />{{Rp|6}} Levasseur was not consistent, however; a dozen of the signs translate "indifferently", meaning sometimes the first letter of the digraph is not removed, for example a sign representing "il" may only show as "i" or "l". This may have been due to a difficulty on the part of the [[Encryption|encrypter]] in telling apart certain [[Letter (alphabet)|letters]] or [[number]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pelling |first=Nick |date=30 March 2015 |title="La Buse"'s Cryptogram And French Love Magic? |url=https://ciphermysteries.com/2015/03/30/la-buses-cryptogram-and-french-love-magic |access-date=7 June 2025 |website=Cipher Mysteries |ref=NPCRYPT}}</ref> Some signs also represent a letter or a number, with no clear distinction, their meaning instead determined by context and placement within the text. Ambiguity plays a deliberate part in the composition of the cryptogram.<ref name="Roncière-1934" />{{Rp|6}}<ref name="Bath-2013"/>

===La Roncière's decryption===
Pages eight and nine offer an attempted decryption of the cryptogram, written line by line in French on the eighth page and the cryptogram in full presentation on the ninth page. Whilst mostly matching more modern versions, La Roncière's decryption deliberately leaves out certain letters, instead leaving it up to the reader to "guess" the parts that are not filled in. The decryption in ''Le Flibustier Mystérieux'' is written as follows:<ref name="Roncière-1934" />{{Rp|8–9}}

  <!-- image 1 -->

<blockquote>
<poem style="font-style:italic; margin:1em 0">{{lang|fr|1. I. Prenez une paire de pijon virez les
2.  2 cœurs... tête cheval... une kort
3.  fil winshient écu prenez une cullière
4.  de mielle .. outre vous en faites une ongat
5.  mettez sur le pasage de la .........
6.  ........... prenez 2 liv cassé sur le ch-
7.  (ch)emin, il faut ..... toit à moitié couvé
8.  pour empecher une femme ....... vous n'avé
9.  qu'à vous sere la ........... pour ve-
10.  nir ........ épingle ... juilet .....
11.  ........ faire piter un chien turq un
12.  ..... de la mer.. bien sèche et sur
13.  ................... k'unne femme q-
14.  (qu)i veut se faire d'un ..............
15.  dans ......... dormir un homm(e) r
16.  ......... faut rendre ... q
17.  (q)u'un diffur (?) ..................
}}
</poem>
</blockquote>From these 17 lines, Le Roncière extrapolates on the words from the decrypted cryptogram, describing them as strange "bizarreries" and hypothesising on who the encrypter could be. He quickly establishes that the encrypter is likely of French origin, specifically the [[Grand Est|North-East of France]], one factor being attributed to the harsh pronunciations of certain words. Both 'kort' (line 2) and 'k'unne' (line 13)—despite neither originating from French—can be derived from {{langx|fr|'corde'|lit=rope}}. Moreover, 'piter' (line 11) can be synonymised to bitter, which means to roll a rope around the 'bitte' of a ship ('[[Bitts|bitt]]' in English being the nautical post used to secure [[Mooring|mooring rope]]). On the twelfth line, two points following the word {{langx|fr|'mer'|lit=sea}} are described by La Roncière as being easily replaced. These are not elaborated on, instead being left to the reader to guess.<ref name="Roncière-1934" />{{rp|8}}

===Possible location of Levasseur's treasure===
Using a drawn map of an island, on page ten La Roncière begins "controlling" the [[cryptogram]]'s data, matching words to various things that provide "clues" as to the location of [[Olivier Levasseur#The treasure|Levasseur's treasure]]. 'Les deux cœurs' meaning 'the two hearts' (line 2) is attributed by La Roncière to a matter of {{langx|fr|"virer"|lit=drawing}}, as in 'drawing' meaning 'to arrive' at the {{langx|fr|"tete de cheval"|lit=the horse head}}. La Roncière then mentions a roughly drawn out [[glacier]] to the south, where {{langx|fr|"la chien turc"|lit=a Turkish dog}} and {{langx|fr|"le toit à moilié couvé"|lit=a half-covered roof}}{{efn|Written as 'coupe' in this paragraph.}} are located. Finally La Ronciere lists what he describes as an "abundance of rock engravings" from the surrounding area including a {{langx|fr|"lézard, tortue, chien patte levée, toit pointu, œeil du monstre, deux ailes"|lit=lizard, turtle, dog with a raised paw, a pointed roof, the eye of a monster, two wings}}.<ref name="Bath-2013"/> Altogether, these excerpts from the cryptogram describe the location of where the [[privateer]]s stayed.<ref name="Roncière-1934" />{{rp|10}}

With this cryptic information extrapolated from the cryptogram, La Roncière questions where this mysterious island could be. He states that they have "astronomical data that denotes the trained eye of a seasoned [[sea captain]]", providing the reader with the following data:<ref name="Roncière-1934" />{{rp|10}}

<blockquote>
'' 'Pr N nord 24 B 39 Pas 2° sud — 2° sud S T 62.39 jaites 3 toises.' ''
</blockquote>

La Roncière attributes this data to one of the cryptogram's aforementioned [[petroglyph]]s, the "half-cut roof". The latitude is said not to match, with the exact map plotted questioned also.<ref name="Roncière-1934" />{{rp|10}} Reference is made to the first accurate map of the Indian Ocean, published by {{ill|Jean-Baptiste d'Après de Mannevillette|fr|Jean-Baptiste d'Après de Mannevillette}} in ''Le Neptune oriental'' during the latter half of the 18th century, decades after the privateers disappeared. La Roncière states that longitude was so difficult to determine before the 20th century that God had "forbidden human knowledge of it" and reasons that without the [[chronometers]] of the day or instantaneous [[wireless telegraphy]] to determine the [[Meridian (geography)|meridian]] to within a few metres (consequently verifying geologist [[Alfred Wegener]]'s hypothesis on [[continental drift]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wegener |first=Alfred |url=https://dn790002.ca.archive.org/0/items/dieentstehungder00wege/dieentstehungder00wege.pdf |title=Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane |publisher=F. Vieweg & Sohn |year=1920 |edition=2nd completely revised |series=Die Wissenschaft: Einzeldarstellungen aus der Naturwissenschaft und der Technik |volume=66 |location=Braunschweig |language=de |access-date=15 June 2025}}</ref>{{clarify|date=October 2025}}), locating the treasure using the intersection of latitude and longitude would be an "illusory investigation". Instead, on page eleven, La Roncière uses a [[rebus]] to attempt further placement of the treasure:<ref name="Roncière-1934" />{{rp|10–11}}

<blockquote>
<poem style=font-style:italic>
'P<sup>r</sup> I<sup>er</sup> pas<sup>se</sup> avec p<sup>re</sup> de pqtx
En prendre L 2 V L f S N I C<sup>lot</sup> de même
Et de L S<sup>ce</sup> E f<sup>re</sup> l<sup>a</sup> ge Cm Io gat L m<sup>e</sup>
Sur 1'0 : pge de la source
p<sup>r</sup> I h<sup>2</sup> 8 C<sup>a</sup> ghe p<sup>s0</sup> pour L ch de la M<sup>e</sup>
B<sup>n</sup> ghe L frote C<sup>tre</sup> la p<sup>se</sup> S<sup>rd</sup> g L V t q<sup>e</sup>
p<sup>ser</sup> cher S f<sup>re</sup> X d l<sup>de</sup> L D g<sup>lo</sup> D L<sup>o</sup>
D du C<sup>ble</sup> du C<sup>eur</sup>.'
</poem>
</blockquote>

{{Langx|fr|"La plage de la source"|lit=The beach at the source}} is indicated to be a [[Sacred spring|spring]] near the sea, located within the estate of the aforementioned landowner, who allegedly passed Levasseur's documents to the young woman. Unfortunately, the "ingenious" explanation given by the landowner to La Roncière for the petroglyphs is not shared with the reader out of discretion. The {{Langx|fr|"C<sup>ble</sup> du C<sup>eur</sup>"|lit=cable of the heart}} is also mentioned by La Roncière, "cable" being interpreted as a [[length measurement|measurement of length]] meaning height, and "heart" meaning a person in control. Put together, "cable of the heart" could refer to "height of the Commander". Another interpretation is that "the heart" could be interpreted as "the Curator", a title held by a French [[Captain|pirate leader]]. Both of these conclusions are left open-ended for the reader's deliberation. La Roncière adds further context to the reading of "the Commander", which he says is understood to mean the foreman of [[Atlantic slave trade|enslaved Africans]] (described in the novel as "Negroes"). La Roncière attributes this to the historical English pirate [[Henry Every]],{{efn|Referred to as "John Avery" in ''Le Flibustier Mystérieux''.}} who owned a number of slaves, and whom the latter half of the novel focuses on.<ref name="Roncière-1934" />{{rp|11}}

==Search attempts==
===Reginald Cruise-Wilkins and Savy family's search at Bel Ombre===
During the 19th century, the Savy family of [[Mahé, Seychelles]], came into possession of Levasseur's papers. The information they extracted from the papers led them to [[Bel Ombre, Mauritius]]. Here, at the [[National Archives of Mauritius]], they discovered other scarcely seen papers containing Levasseur's cryptogram. From 1913 onwards, the Savy family excavated the beach at Bel Ombre.<ref name="The Townsville Daily Bulletin-1950" /> It was during this time that an unidentified [[cryptographer]] studied the cryptogram finding no solution until Charles de La Roncière's publication in 1934.<ref name="Roncière-1934" /> Fourteen years later in 1948, former [[King's Guard]] and Kenyan settler Reginald Cruise-Wilkins visited [[Seychelles]] during a holiday. Unable to return home until another boat departed three months later, he chose to reside at Bel Ombre. Cruise-Wilkins was shown Levasseur's cryptogram by Mrs Charles Savy of the Savy family and the unidentified cryptographer. Using the information they had learned, along with the [[petroglyph]] identifiers from La Roncière's work, Cruise-Wilkins became set on finding Levasseur's treasure, which he believed was located under the beach at Bel Ombre.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Treasure Site |url=https://www.seyheritage.sc/heritage-sites/treasure-site |access-date=24 June 2025 |website=Seychelles Heritage Foundation |ref=SHFTS}}</ref><ref name="Soteriou-2017">{{Cite web |last=Soteriou |first=Helen |date=27 August 2017 |title=The island with £100 million hidden |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/travel/article/20170425-the-island-with-100-million-hidden |access-date=24 June 2025 |publisher=BBC Travel |ref=BBCRCW}}</ref>
[[Image:Seychelles 003.JPG|right|thumb|A beach located on the island of [[Mahé, Seychelles]]]]

In 1949, Cruise-Wilkins enlisted the help of retired [[Indian Army]] officer Colonel D. M. Hennessey, after seeing an advert by him in a local paper offering services for [[Dowsing|water divination]]. After a year, they were unable to locate anything of note.<ref name="The Townsville Daily Bulletin-1950" /> From 1951 to 1955, Cruise-Wilkins continued to dig under a giant rock he named "the glacis", funded by an investment from the [[Government of Seychelles]]. Previously having funded the search himself and with help from his mother, by 1955 Cruise-Wilkins had run out of money. Under Kenyan accounting firm Gill and Johnson, he managed to secure £24,000 from 400 [[shareholders]], each of whom would receive a share of his percentage (with the other divisions going to the Seychelles Government) should the treasure be discovered. The [[Prospectus (finance)|prospectus]] was subsequently authorised.<ref name="Fleming-1958" /><ref name="The Townsville Daily Bulletin-1950" /> Returning to Bel Ombre, Cruise-Wilkins continued to search, with updates being provided to shareholders in Kenya by Colonel J. Kent, an arrangement which ended in 1957.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Fleming |first=Ian |date=31 August 1958 |title=Treasure Hunt in Eden—3 |url=https://quarterdeck.commanderbond.net/t/ian-flemings-adventure-journalism/1417/30 |access-date=25 June 2025 |work=[[The Sunday Times]]}}</ref> Reginald Cruise-Wilkins continued to search for Levasseur's treasure at Bel Ombre until his death in 1977.<ref name="Soteriou-2017" />

===Continued searches by John Cruise-Wilkins and Robert Graf===
Reginald Cruise-Wilkins' son John continued the search in 1988 after obtaining the required permits from the government. Carrying on in the same area of Bel Ombre, John Cruise-Wilkins used modern equipment including pumps, drills, jackhammers, excavators and blasting, along with hand tools where necessary.<ref name="Soteriou-2017" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=11 January 2021 |title=A Brit on the biggest pirate treasure hunt ever in Seychelles |url=https://www.wantedinafrica.com/news/a-brit-on-the-biggest-pirate-treasure-hunt-ever-in-seychelles.html |access-date=25 June 2025 |website=Wanted in Africa |ref=WIAJCW}}</ref> Four years prior to resuming the search, former [[US Air Force]] technical instructor Robert Graf moved to [[Mahé, Seychelles|Mahé]] and joined the project, contributing both to funding and locating the treasure. Graf and Cruise-Wilkins broke off to search in different locations after four years of searching. During the 1990s and early 2000s, they alternated licensing periods to expand the search further. By comparing markings on the rocks at Mahé, Graf was able to construct a lagoon, furthering his excavation between Cruise-Wilkins' search periods. Twelve petroglyphs located by Graf were interpreted as aligning with specific comments in Levasseur's papers, with one photo revealing a sequence of holes mirroring a [[constellation]] referred to in Levasseur's writings. Prior to this, the number 62 was found to be referenced in Levasseur's papers, matching a [[Domino|domino game piece]] found by Cruise-Wilkins, with handmade inlays showing a six and two close to where Graf was searching at the time.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Behar |first=Michael |date=December 2004 |title=Treasure Quest |url=https://www.michaelbehar.com/articles/smithsonian-treasure-quest/ |access-date=25 June 2025 |magazine=Smithsonian Magazine |pages=116–121 |volume=35 |issue=9 |ref=MBTQ}}</ref> Graf and Cruise-Wilkins continued their excavation work on alternating licenses until 2009, at which point the [[Government of Seychelles]] mandated that a 250,000 [[Seychellois rupee]] licence fee must be fulfilled to be able to continue the search.<ref name="Soteriou-2017" />

==Authenticity==
===Of historical events===
Many sources on the subject exercise some degree of poetic license by mixing fictional events with people and events that did exist, which makes it difficult to validate what is and is not true. It is generally accepted by historians that Olivier Levasseur likely partook in the 1721 raid on the ''Nossa Senhora'', which at the time was indeed transporting the [[Luís de Meneses, 1st Marquis of Louriçal|Viceroy of Goa]]. Whilst a large amount of high-value "treasure" was taken by Levasseur and his associates, it is understood that much of his associates' shares were given to Spanish [[Portobelo]] in return for [[amnesty]] for the crime. The Fiery Cross of Goa is believed to be part of the legend as attested to in La Roncière's novel, with cynicism given to treasure hunters who continue to search for it today.<ref name="Dahlke-2024" />{{rp|8}} According to some sources, Levasseur reportedly kept his share. In 1730, when Levasseur was captured, many sources suggest he threw a piece of paper into the crowd, although this claim is not present in contemporary literature.<ref name="Dahlke-2024" />{{rp|7}} This part of the legend is generally considered to have been fabricated within ''Le Flibustier Mystérieux'' by Charles de La Roncière, who admitted within his novel that he did not like the governor's version of Levasseur's execution, instead preferring the version with the cryptogram.<ref name="Dahlke-2024" />{{rp|3}}<ref name="Roncière-1934" />{{rp|108f}}

===Of the cryptogram===
Levasseur's cryptogram is generally agreed to have originated within La Roncière's novel ''Le Flibustier Mystérieux''. All publications discussing the cryptogram after this novel refer back to La Roncière's writings and no mention of a manuscript containing a cryptogram is known to have existed before this. The novel's publishing house La Masque was known for publishing [[Fiction writing|fictional works]] and satire, and it is likely La Roncière would have chosen a different publisher if he intended the novel to be a genuine historical work of non-fiction.<ref name="Dahlke-2024" /> It has also been questioned why a notable historian such as La Roncière would publish a novel about a cryptogram where no evidence exists linking it to Levasseur directly.<ref>{{Cite web |title=La Buse Cryptogram |url=https://cipherfoundation.org/older-ciphers/la-buse-cryptogram/ |access-date=26 June 2025 |website=The Cipher Foundation |ref=TCFLBC}}</ref> It is possible a document was shown to La Roncière which was then attributed to Levasseur, though no physical evidence for this has ever surfaced. [[Robert Charroux]]'s 1962 book ''Treasures of the World'' introduced Mrs Savy, descendant and [[Inheritance|inheritor]] of the pirate Nageon de L'Estang.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Charroux |first=R. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sBP_swEACAAJ |title=Treasures of the World |publisher=Muller |year=1966 |access-date=26 June 2025}}</ref> Unfortunately, no direct evidence of a document containing the cryptogram being passed from the Savy family to La Roncière has ever been found to exist. Charroux's publications are known to be questionable, and no information regarding where this information was obtained is known. This leaves the origin of Levasseur's cryptogram a likely invention of 20th-century fiction.<ref name="Dahlke-2024" />
